figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of Visual Token Routing (VTR). Spatio-temporal router: A lightweight router reads each image region across the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. Zoomed-in region: While the agent types a file name into a save dialog in front of a playing video, the router keeps only the tokens of the typed file name. It drops the regions that did not change, and also drops the circled part of the video, which changed but is not relevant to the task.
figures.headline: The router keeps the typed file name in a save dialog and drops unchanged regions and a changed video region irrelevant to the task.
citing_sentences: Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction (§2; Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Where the router acts. The first observation of each block is an anchor and is kept in full, while the router keeps only some regions, shown shaded, of the other observations in the block.
figures.headline: Anchor observations are kept in full, while the router keeps only some regions of each later observation in its block.
citing_sentences: We group observations into blocks of $B$ consecutive observations and call the first observation of each block an anchor (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Training in VTR. Joint training: We train $\pi_{\theta}$ and the router together with the cross-entropy (CE) loss on the kept tokens, and also train the router to keep fewer tokens with $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{deg}}$. The full and blind models see all tokens and only the anchors, and are used only during training. Measuring degradation: We compare the losses of the three models to measure how much the full history helps ($i_{n}$) and how much dropping tokens hurts ($d_{n}$). Adaptive weight $\lambda$: We increase $\lambda$ when the share of this help that $\pi_{\theta}$ loses, $\bar{r}$, exceeds the small tolerance $r^{\star}$, so that the router keeps more tokens, and decrease it otherwise.
figures.headline: Joint training updates the model and router with cross-entropy on kept tokens, while the router also minimizes kept tokens against degradation.
citing_sentences: Training the router requires balancing two goals: keeping as few visual tokens as possible and preserving the accuracy of action prediction (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: VTR matches full-resolution performance with far fewer visual tokens. Score on OSWorld (left), average score on CUA-World (middle), and click accuracy in video games (right), against visual tokens per image. The dashed line marks the dense model at full resolution.
figures.headline: VTR reaches the dense model's score on OSWorld and CUA-World and its game click accuracy with fewer visual tokens per image.
citing_sentences: With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model in all three domains, while using 2.5-5.8$\times$ fewer visual tokens (Figure 4).
Figure 4 compares VTR with the dense model, which processes every visual token, across numbers of tokens per image.

Figure 4 also compares VTR with two other ways to reduce visual tokens: lowering the image resolution, and hand-designed rules that keep the regions that changed between observations, namely pixel-diff and H.264.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: VTR makes inference cheaper and faster. Score on OSWorld (left), average score on CUA-World (middle), and click accuracy in video games (right), against inference cost relative to the dense model at full resolution (top) and prefill time per step (bottom). The dashed line marks the dense model at full resolution.
figures.headline: VTR keeps the dense model's score on each benchmark while lowering inference cost and prefill time relative to the full-resolution model.
citing_sentences: These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3$\times$ and speed up prefill by up to 2.9$\times$ (Figure 5).
Figure 5 shows the performance of each method against its inference cost and its prefill time, the time the model takes to process its input before generating an action.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: VTR adapts how many visual tokens it keeps to each domain and game. Percentage of visual tokens kept by each method on desktop tasks and on video games grouped by how much of the screen changes between consecutive frames.
figures.headline: VTR keeps 2.7% of tokens in low-motion games, 5.9% in high-motion games, and 26.3% on desktop tasks.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 shows the percentage of visual tokens each method keeps.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: VTR keeps only the regions that the agent needs. The previous observation (top) and the current observation with the regions that VTR drops dimmed (bottom), in three video games and a desktop application.
figures.headline: In Dota 2, VTR keeps 23 of 220 regions, mostly fighting units and health bars, and dims the static map.
citing_sentences: To see which regions the router keeps, Figure 7 shows the previous observation and the regions that VTR keeps in the current one.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Further examples of the regions that VTR keeps. For each example, the previous observation (left) and the current observation with the regions that VTR drops dimmed (right), in video games and desktop applications.
figures.headline: Further game and desktop examples show VTR dimming static background while keeping selected changed regions.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 shows further examples of the regions that VTR keeps, in video games and desktop applications.

abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent’s next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8$\times$ fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3$\times$ and speed up prefill by up to 2.9$\times$. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost.

sections.body: Computer-use agents keep each 1080p screenshot as about 2,000 visual tokens with Qwen3.5, so a 100-step task reaches over 200,000 visual tokens. The paper observes that most of these tokens are either irrelevant to the next action or repeated across screenshots. **Visual Token Routing (VTR)** trains a lightweight spatio-temporal router jointly with the vision-language model. For each image region across the current and previous screenshots, the router decides whether its token enters the language model, and dropped tokens are removed from the input. With 2,000 training steps, VTR matches full-resolution performance on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction using 2.5-5.8 times fewer visual tokens. On OSWorld it outperforms lower resolution by up to 12.8 points, and joint training adds 13.2 points over a separately trained router.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Computer-use agents spend thousands of visual tokens per screenshot, and most of them do not affect the next action.

sections.body: The router takes each image region in the current observation together with the K previous observations at the same position, and a small MLP outputs a keep probability. A Bernoulli gate samples whether the token is kept, and kept tokens are scaled by their keep probability so the loss gives the router a gradient. Every block of B observations starts with an anchor that is kept in full. The degradation loss weights token dropping by how much the full history improves on the anchors alone. A multiplier lambda is updated by dual ascent so that the fraction of lost improvement stays at or below the target r*. The router is first trained on labels from pixel change and object segmentation. A sliding variant drops periodic anchors and reuses the same trained router.
sections.heading: Visual Token Routing
sections.headline: A spatio-temporal router samples keep-or-drop gates per visual token and is trained jointly with the model under an accuracy target.

sections.body: One Qwen3.5-2B model is trained on CUA-World desktop trajectories and on 30 frames per second game recordings from the markov-ai/gaming-500-hours dataset. The router is a three-layer MLP with 23.3M parameters, about 1% of the language model. It reads 10 previous observations, places an anchor every 10 observations, and uses a degradation target of 0.1. Desktop screenshots are 1920×1080 with 2,040 visual tokens. Game frames are 640×360 with 220 visual tokens, and action prediction is evaluated on held-out recordings from 36 games. Baselines are lower resolution at 50%, 25%, and 12.5% of area, pixel-diff, a motion and residual rule from a video codec, and a frozen router. All use the same model and training data.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Qwen3.5-2B is trained on desktop and game data and compared with lower resolution, pixel-difference, codec-based, and frozen-router baselines.

sections.body: On OSWorld, VTR scores 18.1, and it matches the dense model at full resolution on CUA-World and game click accuracy. The router keeps about 40% of tokens on OSWorld and 17% in video games, without a fixed budget. At half the image area, the dense model scores lower than VTR, which scores 2.9 points higher on OSWorld while using fewer tokens. Pixel-diff scores 5.3 and H.264 scores 9.4 on OSWorld. The frozen router scores 4.9, so training the router jointly with the model matters. The section does not report the cause of the frozen router's gap beyond the initial rule it inherits.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: VTR matches full-resolution scores on OSWorld, CUA-World, and game clicks with 2.5-5.8 times fewer visual tokens.

sections.body: Training-free methods keep tokens with the most attention, merge similar tokens, or drop repeated video frames, often using pixels or video codecs. Learned token selectors also exist, but these methods set the number of kept tokens as a ratio, a threshold, or a target count. For computer-use agents, prior methods either discard older screenshots entirely or use fixed rules or a selector trained separately from the action model. Learned routing methods such as mixture-of-experts adjust computation, but they fix its amount or calibrate it after training. VTR instead trains its router jointly with the language model and minimizes kept tokens while preserving accuracy during training.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier token reduction methods fix the kept-token count in advance or train their selector apart from the action model.

sections.body: VTR is a joint training framework that routes visual tokens for computer-use agents while keeping as few tokens as possible without losing accuracy. It matches the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction with 2.5-5.8 times fewer visual tokens. Inference cost falls by up to 3.3 times, and prefill speeds up by up to 2.9 times. The paper reports that learning token selection jointly with the model is crucial. The router sets its own kept count for each input and domain. The conclusion states that this makes long-horizon and real-time use possible at a fraction of the computational cost.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: VTR lets computer-use agents process only the visual tokens they need, cutting inference cost by up to 3.3 times.

sections.body: Training uses 4,265 CUA-World computer-use examples and 29,401 video game examples, sampled at a ratio of 1:3. The router's layers have sizes 22,528, 1,024, 256, and 1, for 23.3M parameters. Initialization labels mark a region as changed when its mean absolute pixel change is at least 10 out of 255. Table 1 lists joint-training settings, including 2,000 training steps, batch size 32, and degradation target 0.1. OSWorld uses 295 of 369 tasks, averaged over three seeds. Video game evaluation covers about 90,000 actions from 36 games. Table 2 gives full OSWorld and CUA-World results, Table 4 gives per-action game accuracy, and Table 3 reports paired t-tests with small, non-significant differences.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists training data, router architecture, joint-training hyperparameters, baseline settings, evaluation protocols, and extra result tables.
